summary: When the Tribunal receives a request to close down a company, it has the power to dismiss the request, make temporary orders, appoint a temporary liquidator, or order the closure of the company. The Tribunal must generally make its decision within ninety days and usually gives the company a chance to speak before appointing a temporary liquidator. Additionally, the Tribunal cannot refuse to close a company just because the company has no assets or its assets are fully mortgaged.
points: The Tribunal may dismiss the winding up petition with or without costs.
The Tribunal may make any interim order or any other order as it thinks fit.
The Tribunal may appoint a provisional liquidator before making a final winding up order.
The Tribunal may order the winding up of the company with or without costs.
The Tribunal must normally give the company notice and a chance to speak before appointing a provisional liquidator.
The Tribunal can refuse a winding up order if another remedy is available and the petitioners are acting unreasonably.
example: A petition was filed by a group of shareholders to wind up Radiant Electronics Private Limited. The Tribunal reviewed the case and decided to appoint a provisional liquidator to manage the company's affairs temporarily until a final closure order could be made. Before doing so, the Tribunal gave Radiant Electronics Private Limited a fair chance to present its side of the story. Later, some creditors objected because the company's assets were fully mortgaged to a bank. However, the Tribunal clarified that it cannot refuse to wind up the company solely on the ground that the assets are mortgaged or that no assets remain.
